\chapter{More Verbs at the Core}
\label{ch:pt-more-core-verbs}

\section[pensar]{pensar — thinking, and the scales it came from}

\label{lesson:PT-C19-pensar}



\begin{quote}
The last chapter gave you the nine verbs Portuguese cannot do without. This one adds eight more, and the first of them weighs things.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: A plain -ar verb, and the small word after it}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{penso} & nós \textbf{pensamos} \\
tu \textbf{pensas} & vocês/eles \textbf{pensam} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{pensa} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

No surprises in the endings: \emph{pensar} runs exactly like \emph{falar}, the first verb you met. What has to be learned is the word that follows it. Portuguese thinks \textbf{in} a thing, not about it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Penso em ti.} — \textquotedblleft{}I think of you.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Penso que sim.} — \textquotedblleft{}I think so.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Pensar em} for whatever you have in mind; \emph{pensar que} for an opinion. In everyday Brazilian speech the opinion verb is more often \textbf{achar} — \emph{acho que sim} — a verb whose plain meaning is \textquotedblleft{}to find.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pensar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{pēnsāre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to weigh out carefully,\textquotedblright{} built on \emph{pendere}, \textquotedblleft{}to hang\textquotedblright{} — because a Roman weighed a thing by \textbf{hanging} it from a balance. To think, on that picture, is to put two things on the scales.

English owns the whole family. From the weighing half: \textbf{pensive}, and \textbf{ponder}, which is \emph{ponderāre} from \emph{pondus}, a weight. From the paying half — coins were weighed out before they were counted — \textbf{pension}, \textbf{compensate}, \textbf{dispense}, \textbf{expense} and \textbf{expend}, \textbf{stipend}, \textbf{recompense}. And from the hanging half: \textbf{pendulum}, \textbf{pendant}, \textbf{pending}, \textbf{depend} (\textquotedblleft{}to hang from\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{suspend}, \textbf{append}, \textbf{impending}. Spanish, another daughter of Latin, put the same verb on its coin: a \emph{\textbf{peso}} is a weight.

\textbf{achar} has its own history — Latin \emph{afflāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to breathe upon,\textquotedblright{} a hunter's word for catching a scent on the air. So the everyday Brazilian \textquotedblleft{}I think\textquotedblright{} is really \textquotedblleft{}I find.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}penso, pensas, pensa, pensamos, pensam\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Penso em ti\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Penso que sim\textquotedblright{}
  \item knowing beside thinking — \textquotedblleft{}sei\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}penso\textquotedblright{}
  \item the weighing family — \textquotedblleft{}pensive · ponder · pension · pendulum\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{pensar}. (\textbf{Penso, pensas, pensa, pensamos, pensam}.) Which small word follows it when someone is on your mind? (\emph{\textbf{Em}} — \emph{penso em ti}.) What did \emph{pēnsāre} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{weigh out}\textquotedblright{}.) So what is a \emph{pendulum} doing? (\textbf{Hanging} — from \emph{pendere}.) And which verb from the last chapter says \textquotedblleft{}I know a fact\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Sei}}.) Next: understanding.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[entender / compreender]{entender / compreender — reaching for it, or grabbing all of it}

\label{lesson:PT-C19-entender-compreender}



\begin{quote}
Weighing a thought was the last lesson. This one is the moment the thought lands — and Portuguese has two verbs for it, built on two pictures.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The everyday one, and the fuller one}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{entender — every day} & \textbf{compreender — a shade deeper} \\
\midrule
\textbf{entendo, entendes, entende, entendemos, entendem} & \textbf{compreendo, compreendes, compreende, compreendem} \\
Não entendo. — I don't understand. & Compreendo a situação. — I grasp the situation. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both are ordinary \emph{-er} verbs, and in most sentences either one is correct. \textbf{Entender} is the workhorse: \emph{Não entendo}, \emph{Entendeu?}, \emph{Entendes?} \textbf{Compreender} carries more weight — understanding a thing through, or taking someone's side of it — and it does a second job English gives to another word entirely: \emph{o preço compreende tudo}, \textquotedblleft{}the price \textbf{includes} everything.\textquotedblright{}

If only one sticks, make it \emph{entender}. \textbf{Não entendo} may be the single most useful sentence a beginner owns.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{entender} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{intendere}}: \emph{in-} (\textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{tendere} (\textquotedblleft{}to stretch\textquotedblright{}). To understand was to \textbf{stretch your attention toward} a thing. English keeps the family whole: \textbf{intend} and \textbf{intention} — the same verb, meaning barely moved — plus \textbf{intense}, \textbf{tend}, \textbf{tendency}, \textbf{tension}, \textbf{extend}, \textbf{pretend} (\textquotedblleft{}to stretch in front\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{contend}, \textbf{attend}, \textbf{portend}. And the things that literally stretch: a \textbf{tent}, a \textbf{tendon}.

\textbf{compreender} $\leftarrow$ \emph{\textbf{comprehendere}}: \emph{com-} (\textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{prehendere} (\textquotedblleft{}to seize\textquotedblright{}). Not reaching this time but \textbf{grabbing}, and grabbing all of it at once — \textbf{comprehend}, \textbf{comprehensive}, \textbf{apprehend}, \textbf{prehensile}. Worn down through French, that same \emph{prehendere} also gives \textbf{prison} (a \textquotedblleft{}seizing\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{prize}, \textbf{enterprise}, and \textbf{surprise}, which is \emph{super-prehendere}, \textquotedblleft{}seized from above.\textquotedblright{}

Flag the false friend: English \textbf{understand} belongs to neither family. It is Germanic, and its own picture is standing close among things.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}entendo, entendes, entende, entendemos, entendem\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Não entendo\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Compreendo a situação\textquotedblright{}
  \item thinking, then understanding — \textquotedblleft{}penso\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}entendo\textquotedblright{}
  \item the stretching family — \textquotedblleft{}intend · intense · extend · tendon\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I don't understand.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Não entendo}}.) Which of the two also means \textquotedblleft{}to include\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Compreender}}.) What does \emph{tendere} mean, and what is \emph{in-tendere} doing? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{stretch}\textquotedblright{}; stretching \textbf{toward} a thing.) Taken apart, what is a \emph{surprise}? (\emph{Super-prehendere} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{seized from above}\textquotedblright{}.) Is English \emph{understand} a relative? (\textbf{No} — it is Germanic.) And \emph{pensar}'s root meaning? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{weigh}\textquotedblright{}.) Next: reading.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ler]{ler — a verb that gathers, worn down to three letters}

\label{lesson:PT-C19-ler}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Ver}, \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} was three letters and irregular. \textbf{Ler}, \textquotedblleft{}to read,\textquotedblright{} is three letters and irregular in exactly the same way — and for the same reason.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: leio, lê, leem}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{leio} & nós \textbf{lemos} \\
tu \textbf{lês} & vocês/eles \textbf{leem} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{lê} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say them slowly. \textbf{Leio} has grown a \emph{y}-glide in the middle. \textbf{Lê} is a single vowel held up by a circumflex. \textbf{Leem} is two \emph{e}'s in a row, and Portuguese pronounces both of them. \textbf{Não leio muito} — \textquotedblleft{}I don't read much.\textquotedblright{}

This is not random damage. It is the very row \emph{ver} uses — \emph{vejo, vês, vê, vemos, veem} — and the one \emph{crer}, \textquotedblleft{}to believe,\textquotedblright{} uses too: \emph{creio, crês, crê, cremos, creem}. Learn the row once and three verbs come with it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ler} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{legere}}, whose first meaning was not reading at all. It was \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to gather, to pick, to choose}.\textquotedblright{} Reading was the metaphor — gathering letters up with the eye — and the metaphor won.

The shrinking is regular, and you have already met it. Latin \emph{legere} lost its \emph{-g-} between vowels, exactly as \emph{manus} lost its \emph{-n-} to give \emph{mão}; that leaves \emph{leer}, whose two vowels then collapse into one. \textbf{Ler} is what is left, and the circumflex on \emph{lê} is the record of the collapse.

English took both halves of \emph{legere}. The gathering half: \textbf{collect}, \textbf{select}, \textbf{elect} (\textquotedblleft{}to pick out\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{intellect} (\textquotedblleft{}to choose between\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{diligent}, \textbf{neglect} (\textquotedblleft{}not to gather up\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{elegant}, which first meant choosy. The reading half: \textbf{legible}, \textbf{lecture}, \textbf{lectern}, \textbf{legend} (\textquotedblleft{}things to be read\textquotedblright{}), and — through French \emph{leçon} — the word \textbf{lesson} itself.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}leio, lês, lê, lemos, leem\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same row for seeing — \textquotedblleft{}vejo, vês, vê, vemos, veem\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Não leio muito\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Não entendo\textquotedblright{}
  \item the gathering family — \textquotedblleft{}collect · select · elect · legend\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{ler}, then the same row for \emph{ver}. (\textbf{Leio, lês, lê, lemos, leem}; \textbf{vejo, vês, vê, vemos, veem}.) What did \emph{legere} mean before it meant \textquotedblleft{}to read\textquotedblright{}, and what went missing on the way to \emph{ler}? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{gather}, to pick, to choose\textquotedblright{}; the \emph{\textbf{-g-}}, between vowels, as in \emph{mão} from \emph{manus}.) Where is that root in English? (\textbf{Legible}, \textbf{lecture}, \textbf{legend}, \textbf{lesson}.) Next: writing.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[escrever]{escrever — scratching, and the e- that props up an s}

\label{lesson:PT-C19-escrever}



\begin{quote}
Reading came last; writing is its partner. And this verb carries a spelling rule that will unlock dozens of other Portuguese words for you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The forms, and a participle you already own}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{escrevo} & nós \textbf{escrevemos} \\
tu \textbf{escreves} & vocês/eles \textbf{escrevem} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{escreve} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A plain \emph{-er} verb, endings identical to \emph{entender}. The irregularity sits elsewhere: the past participle is \textbf{escrito}, never \emph{escrevido}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Já escrevi a carta.} — \textquotedblleft{}I already wrote the letter.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Está escrito.} — \textquotedblleft{}It is written.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Escrito} is the Latin \emph{scriptum} barely touched — which means \textbf{escrito} and English \textbf{script} are one word arriving twice.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{escrever} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{scrībere}}, \textquotedblleft{}to scratch, to incise,\textquotedblright{} because writing began as cutting marks into wax, clay, or bark. Its participle stem \emph{script-} is among the most productive things English ever borrowed: \textbf{scribe}, \textbf{scribble}, \textbf{script}, \textbf{scripture}, \textbf{describe} and \textbf{description}, \textbf{prescribe}, \textbf{subscribe}, \textbf{transcribe}, \textbf{inscribe}, \textbf{ascribe}, \textbf{conscript}, \textbf{circumscribe}, \textbf{postscript} — and \textbf{manuscript}, which is \emph{manus} plus \emph{scriptum}, \textquotedblleft{}written by the hand.\textquotedblright{} Old English borrowed the verb early and wore it down to \textbf{shrive} and \textbf{shrift}, the confession words behind \emph{Shrove Tuesday}.

Now the rule. Latin \emph{scrībere} opens with \emph{sc-}, and Iberian mouths would not start a word that way, so they propped a vowel in front of it. It happened without exception:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{scrībere} $\to$ \textbf{escrever}
  \item \emph{schola} $\to$ \textbf{escola} (\textquotedblleft{}school\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{stāre} $\to$ \textbf{estar} — the being-verb you already have
  \item \emph{spērāre} $\to$ \textbf{esperar} (\textquotedblleft{}to wait, to hope\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{spatium} $\to$ \textbf{espaço}
\end{itemize}

So when a Portuguese word opens with \textbf{es-} and the rest of it resembles an English word missing its \emph{e}, it usually is one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}escrevo, escreves, escreve, escrevemos, escrevem\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Já escrevi a carta\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Está escrito\textquotedblright{}
  \item reading and writing together — \textquotedblleft{}leio\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}escrevo\textquotedblright{}
  \item the propped-up e — \textquotedblleft{}escrever · escola · estar · esperar\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{escrever}. (\textbf{Escrevo, escreves, escreve, escrevemos, escrevem}.) What is its past participle? (\emph{\textbf{Escrito}} — Latin \emph{scriptum}.) What did \emph{scrībere} mean literally? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{scratch}\textquotedblright{}.) Why \emph{escola} and not \emph{scola}? (Iberian Romance \textbf{propped an e-} in front of \emph{sc-}, \emph{sp-}, \emph{st-}.) Which verb of being got the same treatment? (\emph{\textbf{Estar}}, from \emph{stāre}.) And \textquotedblleft{}I read\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Leio}}.) Next: taking.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tomar / pegar]{tomar / pegar — the two takings}

\label{lesson:PT-C19-tomar-pegar}



\begin{quote}
English \textquotedblleft{}take\textquotedblright{} does everything: take a bus, take a coffee, take a book, take a bath. Portuguese splits the work in two, and the line it draws is easy to feel.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Into your hand, or into you}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{pegar — grasp, catch, grab} & \textbf{tomar — consume, take in} \\
\midrule
\textbf{pego, pegas, pega, pegamos, pegam} & \textbf{tomo, tomas, toma, tomamos, tomam} \\
Pego o livro. — I pick up the book. & Tomo um café. — I have a coffee. \\
Pegar um táxi. — To catch a taxi. & Tomar banho. — To take a bath. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The rule of thumb: if the thing ends up \textbf{in your hand}, it is \emph{pegar}; if it ends up \textbf{inside you} — a drink, a medicine, a bath, a decision — it is \emph{tomar}. Both are ordinary \emph{-ar} verbs, so nothing in the endings is new.

One variety note: Portugal puts an \emph{em} behind \emph{pegar}, \emph{pego no livro}, where Brazil says \emph{pego o livro}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pegar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{picāre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to coat with pitch,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{pix, picis} — the black tar that sealed a ship's hull. To \emph{pegar} a thing was to make it \textbf{stick} to you, and Portuguese still uses that sense straight: \textbf{pegajoso} is \textquotedblleft{}sticky,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{a porta não pega} is a door that will not catch. English took the same \emph{pix} as \textbf{pitch} — the tar, not the musical note, which is a different word altogether.

\textbf{tomar} is the honest gap in this chapter. Nobody has pinned its Latin source down: one proposal is \emph{autumāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to assert,\textquotedblright{} worn away to nothing, another an unrecorded \emph{tumāre}, and neither is settled. A book that dressed a guess up as a root would be handing you a memory hook with nothing behind it. What is certain is that \emph{tomar} is old and Iberian — Spanish carries the same verb with the same spread of senses, and no other Romance language has it at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pego, pegas, pega\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}tomo, tomas, toma\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tomo um café\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Pegar um táxi\textquotedblright{}
  \item having and taking — \textquotedblleft{}tenho um livro\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}pego o livro\textquotedblright{}
  \item the sticking family — \textquotedblleft{}pegar · pegajoso · pitch\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb takes a coffee, and which takes a book? (\emph{\textbf{Tomar}}; \emph{\textbf{pegar}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I have a coffee.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Tomo um café}}.) What did \emph{picāre} mean, and what is \emph{tomar}'s root? (To coat with \textbf{pitch}, so \emph{pegar} is \textquotedblleft{}to make stick\textquotedblright{}; \emph{tomar}'s is \textbf{unknown} — disputed, and named as such.) Now \textquotedblleft{}I have\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I write\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{\textbf{Tenho}}; \emph{\textbf{escrevo}}.) Next: asking.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[perguntar]{perguntar — asking, and the pole in the water}

\label{lesson:PT-C19-perguntar}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{dizer}, \textquotedblleft{}to say.\textquotedblright{} Here is the verb that runs the other way — and a second one beside it, because Portuguese asks a \textbf{question} and asks \textbf{for} a thing with different verbs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: perguntar, and its neighbour pedir}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{pergunto} & nós \textbf{perguntamos} \\
tu \textbf{perguntas} & vocês/eles \textbf{perguntam} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{pergunta} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An ordinary \emph{-ar} verb, with its noun beside it: \textbf{uma pergunta}, \textquotedblleft{}a question.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Posso fazer uma pergunta?} — \textquotedblleft{}May I ask a question?\textquotedblright{} (Portuguese \emph{makes} one.) \textbf{Perguntei pelo João.} — \textquotedblleft{}I asked after João.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Now the neighbour. \textbf{Pedir} is \textquotedblleft{}to ask \textbf{for}\textquotedblright{} — to request, to order. \emph{Pergunto a hora} is asking what the time is; \emph{peço um café} is ordering one. English says \textquotedblleft{}ask\textquotedblright{} for both and loses the difference; Portuguese never mixes them.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{perguntar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{percontārī}}, \textquotedblleft{}to inquire\textquotedblright{} — and the picture inside it is worth the whole lesson. It is \emph{per-}, \textquotedblleft{}through,\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{contus}, \textquotedblleft{}a punting pole.\textquotedblright{} To \emph{percontārī} was to \textbf{push a pole through the water to find the bottom}. Asking is sounding the depth of something you cannot see into.

The road to \emph{perguntar} runs through a hardened \emph{c} and a wandering \emph{r}: \emph{percontare} $\to$ \emph{pergontar} $\to$ \emph{perguntar}. Spanish, another daughter of Latin, moved that \emph{r} one step further forward and says \emph{preguntar}.

A warning about the cousins, because honesty beats a long list: this root left English almost nothing. \emph{Per-} is everywhere — \textbf{perceive}, \textbf{perform}, \textbf{permit} — but \emph{contus}, borrowed into Latin from Greek \emph{kontos}, survives only in technical corners.

\textbf{pedir} does better: Latin \emph{petere}, \textquotedblleft{}to seek, to make for,\textquotedblright{} gives \textbf{petition}, \textbf{appetite}, \textbf{compete}, \textbf{impetus}, \textbf{perpetual}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pergunto, perguntas, pergunta, perguntamos, perguntam\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Posso fazer uma pergunta?\textquotedblright{}
  \item saying against asking — \textquotedblleft{}digo\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}pergunto\textquotedblright{}
  \item the asking-for family — \textquotedblleft{}petition · appetite · compete · impetus\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb asks a question, and which asks for a coffee? (\emph{\textbf{Perguntar}}; \emph{\textbf{pedir}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}May I ask a question.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Posso fazer uma pergunta?}}) What is a \emph{contus}, and what is asking on the Latin picture? (A \textbf{pole}; \textbf{probing the bottom} of something you cannot see into.) Where does \emph{pedir} come from, and what court word did \emph{dizer} leave English? (\emph{Petere}, \textquotedblleft{}to seek\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textbf{appetite}, \textbf{compete}; \textbf{verdict}.) Next: helping.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ajudar]{ajudar — helping, and the j that used to be an i}

\label{lesson:PT-C19-ajudar}



\begin{quote}
Asking came last. This is the verb for when the answer is yes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The forms, and the sentence to keep ready}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{ajudo} & nós \textbf{ajudamos} \\
tu \textbf{ajudas} & vocês/eles \textbf{ajudam} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{ajuda} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An ordinary \emph{-ar} verb. The sound to get right is the \textbf{j}, which is not the \emph{j} of English \emph{jam}: it is the soft buzz in the middle of \emph{measure} and \emph{pleasure}. Say \emph{a-ZHU-dar}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Pode ajudar-me?} — \textquotedblleft{}Can you help me?\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Preciso de ajuda.} — \textquotedblleft{}I need help.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Where that little \emph{me} stands is one of the live differences between the two great varieties: Portugal hangs it on the end with a hyphen, \emph{ajudar-me}; Brazil puts it in front, \emph{me ajudar}. Both are standard where they are spoken. For real trouble, though, the word is not this verb at all — it is \textbf{Socorro!}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ajudar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{adiūtāre}}, the repeating form of \emph{adiuvāre}: \emph{ad-} (\textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{iuvāre} (\textquotedblleft{}to help, to gladden\textquotedblright{}). The picture is of coming toward someone, over and over.

Latin \emph{i} before a vowel was said like English \emph{y}, and that \emph{y} is what hardened into the Portuguese \emph{j}: \emph{adiūtāre} $\to$ \emph{aiudar} $\to$ \textbf{ajudar}. The same change gave \emph{hoje}, \emph{já}, and \emph{janeiro}, the month you already know.

English took the verb by two roads. Through French, where it wore down to \emph{aider}, it arrived as \textbf{aid}, an \textbf{aide}, and \textbf{first aid}. Straight from Latin it also took \textbf{adjutant}, the officer who assists, and \textbf{adjuvant}, a medicine that helps another medicine work.

Four sisters, one verb: Portuguese \emph{ajudar}, Spanish \emph{ayudar}, French \emph{aider}, Italian \emph{aiutare} — all four \emph{adiūtāre}, each worn down its own way.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ajudo, ajudas, ajuda, ajudamos, ajudam\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Pode ajudar-me?\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Preciso de ajuda\textquotedblright{}
  \item asking, then helping — \textquotedblleft{}pergunto\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}ajudo\textquotedblright{}
  \item the soft j — \textquotedblleft{}ajudar · hoje · já · janeiro\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{ajudar}, and say how that \emph{j} sounds. (\textbf{Ajudo, ajudas, ajuda, ajudamos, ajudam}; like the \emph{s} in \textbf{measure}.) Ask someone for help. (\emph{\textbf{Pode ajudar-me?}}) What is \emph{adiūtāre} built from, and what did English take from it? (\emph{Ad-}, \textquotedblleft{}toward,\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{iuvāre}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to help}\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{aid}, \textbf{aide}, \textbf{adjutant}, \textbf{adjuvant}.) And \emph{contus}, in \emph{perguntar}? (A \textbf{pole}.) Next: liking — and the one small word Portuguese insists on.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gostar de]{gostar de — liking, which in Portuguese is tasting}

\label{lesson:PT-C19-gostar}



\begin{quote}
The last verb of the chapter, and the one that catches everybody out. In Portuguese you do not like a thing — you like \textbf{of} it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The forms}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{gosto} & nós \textbf{gostamos} \\
tu \textbf{gostas} & vocês/eles \textbf{gostam} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{gosta} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An ordinary \emph{-ar} verb. Everything hard about \emph{gostar} is the word after it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{gostar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{gustāre}}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to taste}\textquotedblright{} — not to like, but to put a thing in your mouth and judge it. English took it as \textbf{gusto}, \textbf{gustatory}, a \textbf{degustation}, and its opposite \textbf{disgust}: \emph{dis-} plus \emph{gustus}, a bad taste.

So Portuguese holds \textbf{two} verbs that once meant \textquotedblleft{}to taste.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Sapere} became \emph{saber}, \textquotedblleft{}to know,\textquotedblright{} and still tastes in \emph{sabe bem}; \emph{gustāre} became \emph{gostar}. One language, one metaphor, taken twice.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why the \emph{de} is not optional}]
Latin never said \textquotedblleft{}taste a thing.\textquotedblright{} It said \textbf{taste \emph{of} a thing} — \emph{gustāre de} — because a sip comes \textbf{from} what is in front of you, not the whole of it. Portuguese inherited the preposition along with the verb:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Gosto de café.} — \textquotedblleft{}I like coffee.\textquotedblright{} (Word for word: \textquotedblleft{}I taste of coffee.\textquotedblright{}) \textbf{Gosto de você.} — \textquotedblleft{}I like you.\textquotedblright{} (Word for word: \textquotedblleft{}I like \emph{of} you.\textquotedblright{}) \textbf{Gostamos muito de Lisboa.} — \textquotedblleft{}We like Lisbon very much.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The \emph{de} is fixed; dropping it is the mistake that marks a beginner fastest. And \emph{de} fuses with any article it meets — \emph{de + o} = \textbf{do}, \emph{de + a} = \textbf{da}, \emph{de + os} = \textbf{dos}, \emph{de + as} = \textbf{das} — so \textquotedblleft{}I like the wine\textquotedblright{} is \emph{gosto \textbf{do} vinho}, never \emph{de o vinho}.

Spanish, the other Iberian daughter of Latin, escaped the same problem the opposite way: it flips the sentence so the thing liked becomes the subject — \emph{me gusta el café}, \textquotedblleft{}the coffee pleases me.\textquotedblright{} Portuguese keeps \textbf{you} as the subject and hangs the preposition on the object instead.

For the stronger feeling: \textbf{adorar}, which needs no \emph{de} (\emph{adoro café}), and \textbf{amar}, kept mostly for people.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gosto, gostas, gosta, gostamos, gostam\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Gosto de café\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Gosto de você\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Gosto do vinho\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two tasting verbs — \textquotedblleft{}sabe bem\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}gosto de\textquotedblright{}
  \item the whole chapter, first person — \textquotedblleft{}penso, entendo, leio, escrevo, pego, pergunto, ajudo, gosto\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I like coffee,\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}I like the wine.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Gosto de café}}; \emph{\textbf{gosto do vinho}}, since \emph{de + o} fuses to \emph{\textbf{do}}.) Why the \emph{de}, what did \emph{gustāre} mean, and which earlier verb has the same story? (You take a taste \textbf{of} a thing; \textquotedblleft{}to \textbf{taste}\textquotedblright{}; \emph{\textbf{saber}}, from \emph{sapere}.) Now the chapter's eight, in the \emph{eu} form. (\textbf{Penso, entendo, leio, escrevo, pego, pergunto, ajudo, gosto}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
